ctw.title: Coral Reefs
ctw.text: Coral reefs are among the most diverse ecosystems on Earth. Although they [cover] less [than] one percent of the [ocean] floor, they [support] a remarkable [share] of marine life. Each reef [is] built by tiny [animals] called polyps, [which] produce hard skeletons of calcium carbonate. Over [centuries], these skeletons [accumulate] and form large structures.

ctw.title: Sleep and Memory
ctw.text: Sleep plays an important role in how the brain stores information. During the day, the brain [collects] a large [amount] of new experiences. At [night], some of [these] memories are [replayed] and strengthened, [while] others are allowed to [fade]. Researchers [have] found that students who sleep [well] after studying [tend] to remember more.

ctw.title: Early Writing
ctw.text: Writing systems developed independently in several parts of the world. The [earliest] examples come from ancient Mesopotamia, [where] people pressed marks [into] wet clay tablets. At [first], these marks [were] used [mainly] to [record] trade and taxes. [Over] time, the symbols [became] more abstract and could [represent] sounds as well as objects.

daily.title: Library Hours During Final Exams
daily.text: Starting Monday, December 7, the Main Library will stay open 24 hours a day until the end of the final exam period on December 18. During overnight hours (midnight to 7 a.m.), only the first and second floors will be available, and a valid student ID will be required to enter the building. Group study rooms can be reserved for up to three hours at a time through the library website. Please note that the café on the ground floor will close at 10 p.m. as usual.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the notice?
options: To announce a change in library hours
To advertise a new café
To explain how to apply for a student ID
To introduce new study rooms
questions.explain: 第1文で「期末試験期間中は24時間開館する」と告知しており、営業時間の変更が主目的である。

questions.q: What can be inferred about students who visit the library at 2 a.m.?
options: They can buy food at the café.
They cannot use the third floor.
They do not need to show identification.
They can reserve a room for the whole night.
questions.explain: 深夜帯は1階と2階のみ利用可能とあるため、3階は使えないと推測できる。カフェは22時閉店、ID提示は必須、予約は最大3時間である。

daily.title: Messages between roommates
daily.text:
Maya (4:12 p.m.): Hey, are you still at the lab?
Jun (4:15 p.m.): Yeah, the experiment is taking forever. Probably another hour.
Maya (4:16 p.m.): No worries. The plumber is coming at 5 to fix the sink, so I'll be home anyway.
Jun (4:17 p.m.): Oh good, I totally forgot about that. Can you ask him to look at the shower too? The water's been lukewarm all week.
Maya (4:18 p.m.): Sure. Want me to save you some dinner?
Jun (4:20 p.m.): You're a lifesaver.

questions.q: Why will Maya be at home at 5 p.m.?
options: She has finished her experiment.
She is cooking dinner for a guest.
She needs to let a repair person in.
She wants to take a shower.

questions.q: What does Jun mean when he writes, "You're a lifesaver"?
options: He is grateful for Maya's offer.
He thinks Maya fixed the shower.
He is worried about his health.
He wants Maya to come to the lab.
questions.explain: 夕食を取っておこうかという申し出への返答であり、感謝を表す慣用表現である。

daily.title: Message from Campus Housing
daily.text:
Dear Residents of Hartley Hall,

As part of our annual safety inspection, maintenance staff will test the smoke detectors in every room on Thursday between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. You do not need to be present, but please make sure that the area around your ceiling detector is clear. Staff will knock before entering. If you have a medical condition that may be affected by the alarm sound, contact the housing office by Wednesday at noon so that we can schedule a separate time for your room.

Thank you,
Campus Housing

questions.q: What are residents asked to do before Thursday?
options: Stay in their rooms all day
Remove objects near the smoke detector
Replace the batteries in their detectors
Sign up for an inspection time
questions.explain: 「天井の検知器周辺を片付けておくように」とある。在室は不要で、時間予約は持病がある人のみである。

questions.q: Why might a resident contact the housing office?
options: To report a broken alarm
To request a room change
To arrange a different inspection time
To ask staff not to knock
questions.explain: 警報音の影響を受ける持病がある場合、別の時間を設定するため水曜正午までに連絡するよう求めている。

academic.title: The Urban Heat Island Effect
paragraphs: Cities are often several degrees warmer than the rural areas that surround them, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. The difference is usually most noticeable at night. While the countryside cools quickly after sunset, many urban neighborhoods remain warm well into the early morning hours.

Several factors contribute to this pattern. Materials such as asphalt, concrete, and brick absorb large amounts of solar energy during the day and release it slowly after dark. [A] In addition, cities have relatively little vegetation. [B] Plants cool their surroundings through evapotranspiration, a process in which water absorbed by roots evaporates from leaves. [C] Tall buildings also play a role: they trap heat between them and reduce the wind that would otherwise carry warm air away. [D]

The consequences extend beyond discomfort. Higher temperatures increase the demand for air conditioning, which raises energy consumption and, in turn, the emission of greenhouse gases. Heat waves are also more dangerous in cities, particularly for elderly residents and people without access to cooling.

Urban planners have proposed a range of solutions. Planting trees along streets, installing "green roofs" covered with vegetation, and using light-colored paving materials that reflect sunlight can all reduce surface temperatures. Some cities have even restored streams that had previously been buried under roads, since open water helps to cool nearby areas.

questions.q: The word "noticeable" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
options: harmful
obvious
frequent
predictable
questions.explain: noticeable は「目立つ・はっきりわかる」の意味であり、obvious が最も近い。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, how do plants lower temperatures?
options: By blocking wind between buildings
By absorbing solar energy at night
By releasing water vapor from their leaves
By reflecting sunlight away from streets
questions.explain: evapotranspiration（根から吸った水が葉から蒸発する過程）によって周囲を冷やすと説明されている。

questions.q:
Look at the four squares [A], [B], [C], and [D] in paragraph 2. Where would the following sentence best fit?

"As a result, the stored heat continues to warm the air long after the sun has set."
questions.explain: 「蓄えた熱が日没後も空気を温め続ける」は、直前の「素材が日中に熱を吸収し、夜にゆっくり放出する」の結果を述べる文であり、[A]が適切である。

questions.q: Why does the author mention "elderly residents" in paragraph 3?
options: To show that heat waves affect some groups more seriously
To explain why energy use increases in summer
To argue that cities should build more hospitals
To give an example of people who prefer rural areas
questions.explain: 都市の熱波が特に高齢者や冷房のない人々にとって危険であることを示す例として挙げている。

questions.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 4 about streams in some cities?
options: They were originally created by urban planners.
They had been covered during earlier development.
They are the main cause of urban flooding.
They make green roofs unnecessary.
questions.explain: 「以前は道路の下に埋められていた川を復元した」とあるため、過去の開発で覆われていたと推測できる。

academic.title: Seed Dispersal by Animals
paragraphs: Because plants cannot move, they depend on outside forces to spread their seeds. If seeds simply fell beneath the parent plant, the young plants would compete with the parent for light, water, and nutrients. Dispersal over longer distances allows a species to colonize new areas and reduces this competition.

Many plants rely on animals for dispersal. One common strategy is to surround seeds with nutritious fruit. Birds and mammals eat the fruit, and the seeds pass through their digestive systems unharmed. [A] Because animals often travel considerable distances before the seeds are excreted, the seeds may end up far from the parent plant. [B] For some species, passage through an animal's gut actually increases the likelihood that a seed will germinate. [C] Stomach acids can weaken the seed's hard outer coat. [D]

Other plants take a different approach. Their seeds are equipped with hooks or sticky surfaces that attach to the fur or feathers of passing animals. The seeds are carried until they fall off or are removed when the animal grooms itself. Unlike fruit-bearing plants, these species offer no reward to the animals that transport them.

Some relationships are more complex. Squirrels and jays bury nuts and acorns to eat later, but they frequently fail to recover all of them. The forgotten seeds, already planted in soil, are in an ideal position to grow. In this way, animals that appear to be simply consuming seeds may in fact be helping forests to expand.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, why is it disadvantageous for seeds to fall directly beneath the parent plant?
options: The seeds are more likely to be eaten.
The young plants would compete with the parent for resources.
The soil beneath large plants contains no nutrients.
The parent plant releases chemicals that destroy the seeds.
questions.explain: 親株の真下に落ちると、光・水・養分をめぐって親株と競合すると説明されている。

questions.q: The word "considerable" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: dangerous
unknown
substantial
regular
questions.explain: considerable は「かなりの・相当な」の意味であり、substantial が最も近い。

questions.q:
Look at the four squares [A], [B], [C], and [D] in paragraph 2. Where would the following sentence best fit?

"This makes it easier for water to enter and for the seed to begin growing."
questions.explain: 「これにより水が入りやすくなり発芽しやすくなる」は、胃酸が種皮を弱めるという直前の文の結果であり、[D]が適切である。

questions.q: What is the main difference between the plants in paragraph 3 and fruit-bearing plants?
options: Their seeds are larger.
They depend on wind instead of animals.
They give animals nothing in exchange for transport.
Their seeds must pass through an animal's gut.
questions.explain: 第3段落末に「果実をつける植物と異なり、運搬する動物に報酬を与えない」とある。

questions.q: Why does the author mention squirrels and jays in paragraph 4?
options: To show that seed-eating animals can also help plants spread
To explain why some forests are shrinking
To compare the intelligence of mammals and birds
To describe how animals choose which seeds to eat
questions.explain: 種を食べるように見える動物が、埋めた種を回収し忘れることで森林の拡大を助けている例として挙げている。

response.prompt: Do you know if the professor posted the slides from today's lecture?
options: I'll check the course page after class.
The lecture hall is on the second floor.
Yes, I mailed the letter yesterday.
She teaches three classes this term.
response.explain: スライドが掲載されたかを尋ねる質問に対し、「授業後にコースページを確認する」が自然な応答である。

response.prompt: I can't believe the bus was late again this morning.
options: The bus stop is right across the street.
I know. Maybe we should start biking instead.
It usually takes about twenty minutes.
I believe you're right about the answer.
response.explain: 不満の表明に共感し代替案を出す応答が自然である。believe の語に引っかけた選択肢に注意する。

response.prompt: Would you mind if I borrowed your notes from Tuesday?
options: Not at all. I'll send you a copy tonight.
Yes, I borrowed them last week.
Tuesday is better for me.
My notebook is blue.
response.explain: Would you mind if...? への承諾は「Not at all.（全く構わない）」である。Yes は「嫌だ」の意味になる点に注意する。

response.prompt: Why don't we move the meeting to Friday afternoon?
options: Because the room was too small.
That works for me, as long as it's after two.
We met on Monday.
I don't know why they moved.
response.explain: Why don't we...? は理由ではなく提案を尋ねる表現であり、条件付きで同意する応答が適切である。

response.prompt: The printer in the computer lab is out of paper again.
options: I printed it in color.
There's a box of paper in the front office.
The lab closes at nine.
It's a new computer.
response.explain: 紙切れという問題の指摘に対し、解決策（用紙のある場所）を示す応答が自然である。

conversation.title: A student talks with an academic advisor

lines.text: Hi, Professor Lin. Thanks for seeing me. I wanted to talk about my schedule for next semester.
Of course. What's on your mind?
I'm planning to take Organic Chemistry, but it meets at the same time as the statistics course I need for my major.
I see. Statistics is only offered in the spring, so you should definitely keep that one. Organic Chemistry has a summer section, though.
Really? I didn't know that. Is the summer section as difficult?
It covers the same material, but in six weeks instead of fifteen. So it's intense. Many students find it easier to focus on one subject, though.
That might actually work for me. I'll look into it.

questions.q: What is the student's problem?
options: She failed a chemistry course.
Two courses she wants are scheduled at the same time.
She cannot decide on a major.
The statistics course is full.
questions.explain: 有機化学と専攻に必要な統計学の時間が重なっていることが相談内容である。

questions.q: What does the professor imply about the summer section?
options: It is easier than the regular course.
It is not open to first-year students.
It moves quickly but allows students to concentrate.
It will be canceled next year.
questions.explain: 6週間で同じ内容を扱うため厳しいが、1科目に集中しやすいと述べている。

conversation.title: A student talks with a librarian

lines.text: Excuse me. I'm looking for a book for my history paper, but the catalog says it's checked out.
Let me see. Ah, it's due back in three weeks. Is your paper due before then?
Then I'd suggest two things. First, you can place a recall request. The current borrower will have to return it within seven days.
That might still be too late.
Right. So the second option is interlibrary loan. We can usually get a copy from another university in two or three days.
That sounds better. Do I fill out a form here?
It's online. I'll show you where to find it.

questions.q: Why does the student go to the library desk?
options: To return a late book
To find a book that someone else has borrowed
To ask about a history class
To reserve a study room
questions.explain: レポートに必要な本が貸出中になっていることを相談している。

questions.q: Why does the student prefer interlibrary loan?
options: It is free of charge.
It will probably get him the book sooner.
He does not want to bother the other borrower.
The recall form is too complicated.
questions.explain: リコールは最大7日かかり締切に間に合わない恐れがあるが、図書館間貸出は2〜3日で届くためである。

announcement.title: A professor makes an announcement in class
announcement.text: Before we start, a quick update about Saturday's field trip to the coastal wetlands. Because of the storm forecast, we're moving the trip to the following Saturday, the fourteenth. The bus will still leave from the parking lot behind the science building at eight a.m. Please bring waterproof boots, since some of the trails will be muddy. If you can't make the new date, email me by Wednesday, and I'll give you an alternative assignment.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
options: To cancel the field trip permanently
To change the date of a field trip
To introduce a new assignment
To explain the effects of storms on wetlands
questions.explain: 嵐の予報のため、見学を翌週の土曜日に延期するという連絡である。

questions.q: What should students do if they cannot attend on the new date?
options: Go to the parking lot at eight a.m.
Buy waterproof boots
Contact the professor by Wednesday
Join a different class
questions.explain: 新しい日程に参加できない場合は水曜までにメールすれば代替課題が出されると述べている。

announcement.title: An announcement on campus radio
announcement.text: Attention, commuters. Starting next Monday, the Blue Line shuttle will no longer stop at the Hill Street entrance because of construction on the new student center. Instead, a temporary stop will be located on Maple Avenue, about two blocks east. Shuttles will run every ten minutes during peak hours, the same as before. Updated maps are available on the transportation website and at the information desk in the main lobby.

questions.q: Why is the shuttle stop being moved?
options: The shuttle schedule is being reduced.
A building is being constructed nearby.
Hill Street is closed for an event.
Students requested a new route.
questions.explain: 新学生センターの建設工事のため、Hill Streetの停留所を使わなくなると述べている。

questions.q: What will stay the same?
options: The location of the stop
The name of the shuttle line
How often the shuttles run at busy times
The maps at the information desk
questions.explain: ピーク時に10分間隔で運行するのは従来通りと述べている。

talk.title: A talk in a geology class
talk.text: Today I want to look at how glaciers shape the land. A glacier is basically a huge mass of ice that moves, very slowly, under its own weight. As it moves, it acts a bit like sandpaper. Rocks frozen into the bottom of the ice scrape against the ground beneath it. Over thousands of years, this scraping can carve out deep valleys. You can tell a glacial valley from a river valley by its shape. Rivers tend to cut narrow, V-shaped valleys, while glaciers produce wide valleys with a U shape. Glaciers also carry enormous amounts of rock and soil. When the ice melts, that material is left behind in ridges called moraines. So, if you're hiking and you come across a long ridge of mixed rocks in an area with no ice today, there's a good chance you're looking at evidence of a glacier that disappeared long ago.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How rivers form V-shaped valleys
How glaciers change the shape of the land
Why glaciers are melting today
How to identify different types of rocks
questions.explain: 冒頭で「氷河がどのように地形を形づくるか」を扱うと述べている。

questions.q: Why does the professor compare a glacier to sandpaper?
options: To explain how it wears away the ground
To describe the color of the ice
To show how quickly it moves
To explain why it melts
questions.explain: 氷に取り込まれた岩が地面を削る様子を紙やすりにたとえている。

questions.q: According to the professor, how can a glacial valley be identified?
options: It is narrow and deep.
It has a wide U shape.
It always contains a river.
It is covered with sand.
questions.explain: 川はV字谷、氷河は幅の広いU字谷をつくると対比している。

questions.q: What does the professor imply about a ridge of mixed rocks in an ice-free area?
options: It was probably formed by a river.
It may have been left by a former glacier.
It is a sign that a glacier will form soon.
It is too recent to study.
questions.explain: 現在氷のない場所の混じった岩の尾根は、昔消えた氷河の痕跡（モレーン）である可能性が高いと述べている。

talk.title: A talk in a psychology class
talk.text: Let's talk about something that's directly useful to all of you: the spacing effect. The idea is simple. If you study material in several shorter sessions spread out over time, you'll remember it much better than if you study for the same total amount of time in one long session. Now, cramming the night before an exam can feel effective. You review everything, it all seems familiar, and you feel confident. But that sense of familiarity is a bit misleading. Recognizing information is not the same as being able to recall it on your own. When you space out your study sessions, you partly forget the material between them, and having to retrieve it again strengthens the memory. In other words, a little forgetting is actually helpful. So, my advice: instead of one four-hour session this weekend, try four one-hour sessions across the week.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the talk?
options: Studying in spaced sessions improves memory.
Long study sessions are the most efficient.
Forgetting is a sign of poor study habits.
Students should study only on weekends.
questions.explain: 学習を時間的に分散させると記憶が定着するという「分散効果」が主題である。

questions.q: Why does the professor say cramming can be misleading?
options: It makes students too tired to take the exam.
It creates a feeling of familiarity that is not true recall.
It causes students to study the wrong material.
It is not allowed at most universities.
questions.explain: 一夜漬けは見覚えがある感覚を生むが、それは自力で思い出せることとは違うと述べている。

questions.q: According to the professor, why is some forgetting helpful?
options: It allows students to focus on new topics.
Retrieving forgotten material strengthens memory.
It reduces stress before exams.
It shows which topics are not important.
questions.explain: 少し忘れた内容を再び思い出す作業が記憶を強化すると説明している。

questions.q: What does the professor recommend?
options: Studying for four hours on the weekend
Reviewing only the night before the exam
Dividing study time into several sessions during the week
Taking a break from studying for a week
questions.explain: 週末の4時間1回ではなく、1週間に1時間を4回行うよう勧めている。

build.context: Did you finish the reading for tomorrow's seminar?
build.explain: 主語＋only＋動詞句の基本語順。got through は「読み終える・やり遂げる」。

build.context: Where is the career fair being held this year?
build.explain: 間接疑問文では疑問詞の後が平叙文の語順（主語＋動詞）になる。does は不要。

build.context: Why weren't you in class on Monday?
build.explain: 関係代名詞 that が appointment を修飾する構造。

build.context: What did the professor say about the final project?
build.explain: ask＋人＋to不定詞。asked us submitting とはならない。

build.context: Have you decided which apartment to rent?
build.explain: 現在進行形 be＋still＋-ing の語順。

build.context: Can you tell me when the library closes tonight?
build.explain: 平叙文で答える。疑問文の語順 does it closes は誤り。

build.context: How was the guest lecture yesterday?
build.explain: 比較級 more＋than。過去の時点より前の予想なので過去完了 had expected。

build.context: Is the lab report due this week?
build.explain: 現在完了の受動態 has been＋過去分詞。

build.context: Do you want to join our study group?
build.explain: I'd love to の後は動詞を省略し but で条件を続ける。have to＋原形。

build.context: What do you need from the bookstore?

email.scenario: You are taking Professor Grant's environmental science course. You were sick and missed last week's lab session, in which students collected water samples. The lab report is due next Monday.
points: Explain why you missed the lab
Ask whether you can make up the session or use another student's data
email.model:
Dear Professor Grant,

I hope you are doing well. I am writing because I missed last Thursday's lab session. I had a high fever and was advised by the campus clinic to stay home, and I can provide a note from the clinic if needed.

I understand that the water samples collected in that session are essential for the lab report. Would it be possible for me to make up the session at another time? If that is not practical, could I use data collected by one of my classmates instead?

In either case, I may need a few extra days to complete the report properly. Would you consider extending my deadline to Thursday?

Thank you for your understanding.

Best regards,
Kenji Sato
checklist: 件名・宛名・結びが相手（教授）に合った丁寧さか
3つの要求事項をすべて、それぞれ別の文で扱ったか
依頼表現を複数使い分けたか（Would it be possible...? / Could I...? / Would you consider...?）
理由を具体的に書いたか（いつ・なぜ）
100〜150語程度に収まっているか
時制と冠詞の誤りがないか見直したか

email.scenario: You are the president of a small language exchange club. The club wants to hold an event for international and local students next month, but the room you usually use is too small.
points: Describe the event you are planning
Explain why you need a larger room
Ask about available rooms and how to reserve one
email.model:
Dear Student Activities Office,

My name is Aiko Tanaka, and I am the president of the Language Exchange Club. We are planning a cultural evening on November 20, where international and local students will share food, games, and short presentations about their home countries.

We usually meet in Room 204 of the Student Union, but it holds only 25 people. Since more than 60 students have already said they will attend, we will need a much larger space.

Could you let me know which rooms are available that evening for about 70 people? I would also appreciate information on how to make a reservation and whether there is any fee.

Thank you for your help.

Sincerely,
Aiko Tanaka
checklist: 自己紹介と目的を最初の2文で述べたか
イベントの日時・内容を具体的に書いたか
広い部屋が必要な理由を数字などで示したか
空き状況と予約方法の両方を尋ねたか
100〜150語程度に収まっているか
時制と冠詞の誤りがないか見直したか

discussion.professor: Many universities now record their lectures and post them online. Some educators believe this helps students learn, while others worry that it reduces attendance and engagement. In your opinion, should universities make recordings of all lectures available to students? Why or why not?

students.name: Daniel
students.text: I think recordings are essential. Students who work part-time or have health problems sometimes can't attend, and recordings give them an equal chance to keep up. I also rewatch difficult parts before exams.

students.name: Sofia
students.text: I'm not convinced. When I know a lecture is recorded, I'm tempted to skip it, and I never actually find time to watch it later. Being in the room forces me to pay attention and ask questions.

discussion.model: I understand Sofia's concern about motivation, but I agree with Daniel that universities should provide recordings. The key point, in my view, is that recordings are a supplement rather than a replacement for attending. For example, in my statistics class last year, I attended every lecture but still struggled with some proofs. Being able to pause the recording and go through each step at my own pace helped me far more than my notes did. As for the attendance problem, professors could simply make in-class activities, such as short quizzes or group discussions, part of the final grade. That way, students would still have a clear reason to come to class, while those who genuinely cannot attend would not fall behind.
checklist: 冒頭1文で自分の立場を明確にしたか
他の学生の意見に名前を挙げて触れたか
2人と異なる新しい論点を加えたか
具体例（自分の経験・仮定の例）を入れたか
100語以上で、論理の接続語を使ったか

discussion.professor: Some cities have started to ban private cars from their downtown areas, allowing only pedestrians, bicycles, and public transportation. Supporters say this makes city centers cleaner and safer. Critics argue that it hurts local businesses and makes life harder for some residents. Do you think banning cars from downtown areas is a good idea? Explain your view.

students.name: Ryan
students.text: I support it. Cities that have done this have less air pollution and fewer traffic accidents. People also spend more time walking around and shopping, which can actually help businesses.

students.name: Mei
students.text: It sounds nice, but it isn't fair to everyone. Elderly people and people with disabilities may depend on cars, and delivery companies need access to stores too.

discussion.model: Both Ryan and Mei raise valid points, but I believe a partial ban is more realistic than a complete one. Mei is right that some people truly depend on cars, so a city could still allow access for residents with disabilities, taxis, and delivery vehicles during certain hours, such as early in the morning. At the same time, ordinary private cars could be kept out during the day. What neither of my classmates mentioned is the importance of reliable public transportation. A ban only works if people have a convenient alternative. If a city invests in frequent buses and safe bike lanes before introducing restrictions, residents are much more likely to accept the change and continue visiting downtown shops.

interview.intro: Thank you for taking part in our research project. We're interested in how students use technology for learning. I'm going to ask you a few questions.
questions: First, could you tell me about a digital tool or app that you use often for studying?
Some people say that studying with a smartphone nearby makes it harder to concentrate. What has your experience been?
If you were advising a new student, would you recommend taking notes by hand or on a laptop? Why?
Finally, some universities are considering banning devices in lecture halls. Do you think that's a good idea? Please explain.
tips: 最初の1文で質問に直接答える（I mostly use...）
理由を1つ、具体例を1つ加える
後半2問は意見問題：立場→理由→例→簡単なまとめ
沈黙を避けるつなぎ表現：That's an interesting question. / Let me think...

interview.intro: Hello, and thanks for joining us. We're conducting a study about how people experience life in cities. I'd like to ask you four questions.
questions: To begin, what do you like most about the place where you live now?
Tell me about a time when you had to adjust to living in a new environment.
Many young people move to large cities for work. Do you think this trend is good for smaller towns? Why or why not?
Last question. If your city could make one change to improve residents' quality of life, what should it be, and why?
tips: 最初の1文で質問に直接答える
経験を問う質問は「いつ・どこで・何が・どう感じたか」の順で話す
意見問題は利点と欠点の両面に触れると深みが出る
